title: Alan Greenspan, Legendary Fed Chair Who Shaped the U.S. Economy, Dies at 100
summary: Alan Greenspan, the enigmatic and influential former chair of the Federal Reserve, died Monday at his home in Washington. He was 100. Greenspan steered the U.S. economy for nearly 19 years under four presidents, from Ronald Reagan to George W. Bush, presiding over the longest peacetime expansion in American history. A celebrity among central bankers, Greenspan was known for his cryptic “Fedspeak”—a deliberate, jargon-laden style that often left listeners puzzled. But when he warned of “irrational exuberance” in the stock market during a 1996 speech, global markets shuddered. The phrase became legendary, capturing his ability to move billions of dollars with a single question. Born in New York City, Greenspan was a talented jazz clarinetist and saxophonist who studied at Juilliard before turning to economics. He earned a PhD from New York University and built a career as a private consultant before President Reagan appointed him Fed chair in 1987. His tenure was marked by a bold gamble: he kept interest rates low even as unemployment fell, betting that inflation would stay tame. The bet paid off with a booming economy through the 1990s, but critics argue his easy-money policies also inflated the dot-com bubble and later the subprime mortgage crisis that triggered the 2008 global financial meltdown. Greenspan also championed a light regulatory touch, shaped by his libertarian philosophy and admiration for novelist Ayn Rand. After the 2008 crisis, his reputation was tarnished; he acknowledged before Congress that he had found a “flaw” in his ideology. He was married to NBC News anchor Andrea Mitchell, and the two were a Washington power couple. Comedian Jay Leno once joked that Mitchell, not the first lady, was married to “the most powerful man in the world.” Greenspan’s legacy remains fiercely debated—a master of monetary policy to some, an architect of disaster to others.
why_it_matters: Alan Greenspan's story shows how the ideas and decisions of one person at the top of a central bank can ripple through the global economy—boosting jobs and growth one decade, then contributing to a catastrophic crash the next. For young people, the debate over his legacy is a reminder that economic policy is never just about numbers; it's about real consequences for families, housing, and savings.

background_read: The Federal Reserve, often called 'the Fed,' is the most powerful central bank in the world. Its chair is sometimes described as the second-most-powerful person in the United States because decisions about interest rates affect everything from mortgage payments to global stock markets.

Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' line became a landmark moment in financial history. He was warning that investors might be overvaluing technology stocks, and years later the dot-com bubble burst, erasing trillions of dollars in wealth. The episode showed how a few words from a central banker could rattle the entire world economy.

Greenspan's libertarian beliefs came partly from his friendship with novelist Ayn Rand, who championed radical individualism and opposed most government intervention. That ideology led him to argue that financial markets could mostly regulate themselves—a view many now blame for allowing risky lending practices to spread before the 2008 crash.

After the global financial meltdown, Greenspan admitted before Congress that he had found a 'flaw' in his worldview, a rare public mea culpa from a figure once treated as an economic oracle. His legacy remains deeply split between those who admire his steady management of the 1990s boom and those who see him as a key enabler of the worst crisis since the Great Depression.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue that Greenspan's nimble management helped the US enjoy the longest peacetime expansion ever, with low unemployment and inflation through the 1990s. They credit his willingness to break from orthodox thinking—like keeping rates low when traditional models predicted rising prices—for spreading prosperity and making homeownership more accessible.

Critics say Greenspan's 'easy-money' policies and resistance to regulation directly inflated the dot-com bubble and, more dangerously, the subprime mortgage crisis that led to the 2008 global meltdown. They view his libertarian faith in self-correcting markets as dangerously naive and his belated 'flaw' admission as too little, too late.

Historians and economists are often split but agree that Greenspan transformed the Fed's role. His use of 'Fedspeak' to deliberately obscure communication became a tool for reducing market overreactions, and his long tenure established the Fed chair as a globally watched position. Whether his technique helped or hurt transparency remains a matter of debate.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking – lessons for today's central banks
perspectives.description: Modern central bankers still wrestle with Greenspan's conundrum: how to support growth without creating dangerous asset bubbles. The post-2008 regulatory changes tried to fix some of the system's weaknesses he exposed, but new risks—like shadow banking—echo some of the same problems, showing that Greenspan's struggles are not just history.
